questions.stem: A patient presents with muscle weakness and ECG showing peaked T waves. Labs reveal serum K⁺ = 6.5 m Eq /L. Based on the Nernst equation, which of the following best explains the reduced excitability of muscle cells?

options.label: A
options.text: Decreased extracellular K⁺ → RMP more negative

options.label: B
options.text: Increased intracellular K⁺ → RMP more negative

options.label: C
options.text: Increased extracellular K⁺ → RMP less negative

options.label: D
options.text: Decreased intracellular Na⁺ → RMP less negative

questions.answerText: Increased extracellular K⁺ → RMP less negative
questions.solutionHtml:
f3u.cloudfront.net/ckfinder/files/23804691.png" xss=removed>

• ↑ extracellular K⁺ → less K⁺ efflux → RMP becomes less negative → inactivates Na⁺ channels → ↓ excitability.

questions.stem: A child with hepatosplenomegaly, neurodegeneration, and “cherry-red spot” is found to have accumulation of sphingolipids due to a lysosomal enzyme defect. Which function of lysosomes is impaired here?
questions.solutionHtml: : Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes. Defects (e.g., Tay–Sachs) → accumulation of macromolecules due to impaired degradation.

questions.stem: Which of the following contributes most to the generation of the resting membrane potential in neurons?

options.label: A
options.text: Equal permeability to Na⁺ and K⁺

options.label: C
options.text: Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase and selective K⁺ leak

questions.answerText: Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase and selective K⁺ leak
questions.solutionHtml: : • K⁺ leak channels set RMP near –70 mV, close to K⁺ Nernst potential. • Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase maintains gradient but leak dominates RMP.

questions.stem: The presence of plasma proteins that cannot cross capillary membranes leads to:
questions.solutionHtml: : Negatively charged non-diffusible proteins attract cations (Na⁺), repelling anions → electrolyte imbalance known as Gibbs–Donnan effect.

questions.stem: In a negative feedback system, a high increase in BP has turned out to be a small rise in BP due to baroreceptor activation. This indicates:
questions.solutionHtml: n: Gain = correction / error remaining. Large correction (↓HR) for small error (↑BP) → high gain = effective feedback.

questions.stem: A patient with heat stroke presents with hot dry skin, confusion, and tachycardia. Which mechanism has failed?
questions.solutionHtml: n: Evaporation (sweating) is key in heat loss during hyperthermia. In heat stroke, sweating mechanism fails, leading to dry skin and overheating.

questions.stem: A patient with nephrotic syndrome has hypoalbuminemia and edema. What best explains the edema?
questions.solutionHtml: ↓Albumin → ↓oncotic pull → fluid shifts to interstitium → edema.

questions.stem: Before running a race, a sprinter shows increased HR and ventilation without any muscle activity. This anticipatory response is an example of:
questions.solutionHtml: : Feedforward: response triggered by anticipated need (e.g., before actual exertion), not by error.

questions.stem: A patient with prolonged PT and a normal aPTT is found to have deficiency of a vitamin K–dependent factor. Which factor is most likely deficient?
questions.solutionHtml: : PT reflects extrinsic pathway, where Factor VII is first to be affected by vitamin K deficiency.

questions.stem: A newborn develops hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN) due to Rh incompatibility. Which maternal antibody is responsible?
questions.solutionHtml: n: Only IgG crosses the placenta. In Rh-negative mothers, anti-D IgG attacks Rh-positive fetal RBCs → HDN.

questions.stem: During skeletal muscle contraction, which of the following remains unchanged in length?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • The A band represents the length of thick (myosin) filaments and remains constant during contraction. • I band and H zone shorten. • The sarcomere (Z to Z) shortens.

questions.stem: A patient with cardiomyopathy has impaired stroke volume due to abnormal ventricular filling. This is best explained by which physiological principle?
questions.solutionHtml: : • Optimal sarcomere length (~2.0–2.2 µm) maximizes actin-myosin overlap → maximal tension. • In dilated cardiomyopathy, sarcomeres are overstretched → reduced tension.

questions.stem: Which sarcomeric protein anchors the thick filament to the Z-line and contributes to passive elasticity in muscle?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Titin spans from Z-line to M-line, stabilizing myosin and acting like a spring for passive recoil. • Nebulin is associated with thin filament. • Dystrophin connects cytoskeleton to ECM (not part of sarcomere proper).

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy has calf pseudohypertrophy and Gowers’ sign. The absence of which protein leads to sarcolemma instability in Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Dystrophin links actin to the dystroglycan complex and ECM. Its absence → membrane tears → ↑Ca²⁺ influx → necrosis. • X-linked recessive mutation.

questions.stem: Which type of skeletal muscle fiber is most active in a 5-km marathon runner compared to a 100-m sprinter?

options.label: A
options.text: Type I fibers – high mitochondria, slow-twitch

options.label: B
options.text: Type IIA fibers – glycolytic, low myoglobin

options.label: D
options.text: Type IIx fibers – fatigue-resistant, high myoglobin

questions.answerText: Type I fibers – high mitochondria, slow-twitch
questions.solutionHtml: : • Endurance (aerobic) uses Type I: red, oxidative, fatigue-resistant. • Sprint (anaerobic) uses Type IIb / IIx: white, glycolytic, fatigue-prone.

questions.stem: When a person holds a heavy object without changing muscle length, which type of contraction occurs in the biceps?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Isometric = no length change, tension increases (e.g., holding a suitcase). • Isotonic = length changes: o Concentric (shortening), o Eccentric (lengthening under load).

questions.stem: Tetanus toxin blocks neurotransmission by cleaving which component at inhibitory interneurons?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Tetanus toxin targets inhibitory (GABA/glycine) neurons in spinal cord by cleaving V-SNARE (synaptobrevin) → unchecked excitation → spastic paralysis.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old smoker has muscle weakness that improves with repeated use. Reflexes are reduced. What is the pathophysiological mechanism?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Lambert–Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS): Ab against presynaptic P/Q-type Ca²⁺ channels → ↓ACh release. • Improves with use (build-up of Ca²⁺). • Often paraneoplastic (small cell lung carcinoma). • MG is postsynaptic → worsens with

questions.stemHtml: The graph shown below is a muscle’s mechanical response to increasing stimulus frequency. If the duration from point A to D (single muscle twitch) is 100 ms, what is the minimum stimulation frequency (in Hz) required to produce fused tetanus?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • The time from A to D = one complete muscle twitch duration = 100 milliseconds = 0.1 seconds. • For fused tetanus, the stimuli must be delivered before the muscle relaxes, i.e., at intervals < twitch duration. • So, minimum tetanizing frequency = f = 1 / twitch duration = 1 / 50 msec = 20 Hz

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man accidentally touches a hot stove and immediately withdraws his hand, feeling sharp, localized pain followed by a dull, burning sensation. Which of the following fiber types is responsible for conducting the delayed, dull pain?
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Answer (D)

C fibers

questions.stem: A patient with damage to Meissner’s corpuscles would most likely experience difficulty perceiving which of the following sensations?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Meissner’s corpuscles are rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors in glabrous skin, specialized for fine touch and texture. • Pacinian – vibration; Merkel – pressure; Free nerve endings – pain/temp.

questions.stem: Which of the following sensory modalities is conveyed by the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway?
questions.solutionHtml: : • Dorsal column conveys fine touch, proprioception, and vibration from the ipsilateral body. • Pain/temp – spinothalamic.

questions.stem: A patient reports feeling his amputated limb being touched when his face is stroked. This is most likely due to:
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Phantom limb sensation is due to cortical remapping – neighboring cortical areas take over deafferented areas, leading to referred sensations.

questions.stem: A patient feels pain in his missing toe when the stump is touched. This can be explained by which of the following sensory principles?

options.label: B
options.text: Law of projection and labelled line principle

questions.answerText: Law of projection and labelled line principle
questions.solutionHtml: : • Law of projection: regardless of stimulation site along a pathway, sensation is felt at the receptor’s location. • Labelled line principle: the nature of the sensation depends on the type of nerve fiber, not the stimulus type.

questions.stem: Lesion of which structure in the Papez circuit is most likely to impair emotional memory?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Papez circuit: hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → anterior thalamus → cingulate gyrus → parahippocampal gyrus → hippocampus. • Important for emotion-linked memory (limbic system).

questions.stem: Which hypothalamic nucleus is the master regulator of circadian rhythm and is entrained by light?
questions.solutionHtml: : • The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) receives light input from the retina → synchronizes melatonin release and biological clock.

questions.stem: Electrical stimulation of which brain structure evokes autonomic and emotional signs of fear?
questions.solutionHtml: : • Amygdala is the fear and threat center, linking sensory stimuli to emotional responses. • Lesions → loss of fear, disinhibited behavior (Klüver–Bucy syndrome).

questions.stem: Light striking a rod photoreceptor leads to which of the following changes?

options.label: D
options.text: Closure of Na⁺ channels and hyperpolarization

questions.answerText: Closure of Na⁺ channels and hyperpolarization
questions.solutionHtml: : • Light activates rhodopsin → transducin → ↓cGMP → Na⁺ channels close → hyperpolarization → ↓glutamate release.

questions.stem: A lesion in the lateral lemniscus would most affect which function?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Lateral lemniscus carries auditory information bilaterally to the inferior colliculus, critical for sound localization. • Frequency detection occurs at cochlear level.

questions.stem: Which taste modality is sensed via ion channels rather than G-protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs)?
questions.solutionHtml: : • Sour = H⁺ ions enter via ion channels. • Sweet, bitter, and umami use GPCRs (T1R and T2R families).

questions.stem: A drug that blocks L-type calcium channels will most directly affect which phase of the ventricular myocyte action potential?
questions.solutionHtml: ion: • Phase 2 = plateau, due to Ca²⁺ influx via L-type channels balancing K⁺ efflux. • Blocking these channels shortens AP duration and reduces contraction strength.

questions.stem: A prolonged PR interval on ECG most likely indicates a delay in conduction through which structure?
questions.solutionHtml: on: • PR interval = atrial depolarization + AV nodal delay. • AV node delay allows time for ventricular filling.

questions.stem: The first heart sound (S1) corresponds to which of the following cardiac events?

options.label: A
options.text: Closure of aortic and pulmonary valves

options.label: B
options.text: Opening of mitral and tricuspid valves

options.label: C
options.text: Closure of mitral and tricuspid valves

questions.answerText: Closure of mitral and tricuspid valves
questions.solutionHtml: • S1 = AV valve closure → marks start of systole.

questions.stem: A patient with tricuspid regurgitation would show which of the following JVP changes?
questions.solutionHtml: on: • v wave = atrial filling against closed tricuspid valve. • In tricuspid regurgitation, v wave is exaggerated due to backflow

questions.stem: The dicrotic notch in the aortic pressure waveform represents:
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Dicrotic notch = backflow causing aortic valve closure, seen in early diastole.

questions.stem: Which of the following changes would increase cardiac oxygen consumption the most?
questions.solutionHtml: on: • Tension-time index: myocardial O₂ demand increases most with contractility and afterload. • Contractility increases active work done by the heart.

questions.stem: In a patient with systemic vasoconstriction, a 50?crease in arteriole radius leads to what approximate change in blood flow?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D)

questions.stem: Which of the following changes increases total peripheral resistance in a tissue bed?
questions.solutionHtml: : • In parallel circuits, resistance decreases with more open paths. • Closing vessels → ↑resistance.

questions.stem: In an aneurysmal aortic segment, wall tension increases primarily due to which factor?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Laplace’s Law: Tension = [Pressure x radius] / Wall thickness → ↑ radius → ↑wall tension → risk of rupture.

questions.stem: Sudden standing from supine position activates which reflex to maintain blood pressure?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • ↓venous return → ↓BP → ↓baroreceptor firing → ↑sympathetic outflow → vasoconstriction, ↑HR.

questions.stem: IV infusion rapidly increases venous return. Reflex increase in heart rate is mediated via:
questions.solutionHtml: : • Bainbridge reflex: ↑venous return → RA stretch → ↑HR via vagal inhibition.

questions.stem: Coronary blood flow is lowest during which phase of the cardiac cycle in the left ventricle?
questions.solutionHtml: on: • Systolic compression of left coronary vessels reduces flow. • Flow mainly occurs during diastole in the left ventricle.

questions.stemHtml: A patient undergoes cardiac catheterization to assess his left ventricular function prior to thoracic surgery. What is his ejection fraction, as determined from the left ventricular pressure-volume curve illustrated below.
questions.solutionHtml: n: The ejection fraction (EF) is equal to the stroke volume (SV) divided by the end-diastolic volume (EDV) and the stroke volume (SV) is equal to the end-diastolic volume (EDV) minus the end-systolic volume (ESV). EF = SV/EDV = EDV – ESV/EDV In this case, the end-diastolic volume is 130 mL and the end-systolic volume is 60 mL. Therefore, the ejection fraction is 70 mL/130 mL or 0.54.

questions.stemHtml: Three parallel arterioles arising from an artery and their respective resistances are given in the picture. Due to vasodilation, the resistance of Arteriole B decreases to 15 PRU, while A and C remain unchanged. What is the approximate percentage increase in total vascular conductance of the organ?

A small arteriole normally has a radius of 1 mm. Due to autonomic regulation; the radius decreases by 50%. Assuming no change in pressure or viscosity, by approximately how much does the blood flow through the arteriole change?

questions.stem: A 25-year-old fasting individual experiences rhythmic contractions in the stomach every 90 minutes. Which of the following best explains the physiological role of the hormone involved?

options.label: A
options.text: Stimulates gastric acid secretion during cephalic phase

options.label: C
options.text: Stimulates migrating motor complex during fasting

questions.answerText: Stimulates migrating motor complex during fasting
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Motilin is released cyclically during fasting and stimulates MMC, clearing the gut of residual food and bacteria. • A: Gastrin/HCl related • B: Motilin stimulates, not inhibits • D: Segmentation is promoted by CCK, not motilin

questions.stem: A patient with duodenal ulcer undergoes a test where secretin is administered. Which response confirms intact duodenal physiology?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Secretin is released in response to acidic chyme in duodenum. • Stimulates HCO₃⁻ secretion from pancreas and biliary duct. • A: Secretin inhibits gastric acid • C: Not direct action • D: Somatostatin is not directly suppressed

questions.stem: A cholecystectomy patient is less efficient in digesting fats. Which of the following CCK effects best explains the problem?

options.label: C
options.text: Contracts gallbladder and relaxes sphincter of Oddi

questions.answerText: Contracts gallbladder and relaxes sphincter of Oddi
questions.solutionHtml: n: • CCK is released by I cells in duodenum → promotes bile release and pancreatic enzyme secretion • Without gallbladder, bile delivery is less efficient

questions.stem: Which neurotransmitter predominantly mediates excitatory motor signals in the myenteric plexus?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • ACh → major excitatory NT for gut motility • NO → inhibitory • Dopamine → reduces motility • Somatostatin → inhibitory

questions.stem: Which of the following is true regarding the basal electrical rhythm in the gastrointestinal tract?

options.label: A
options.text: It is generated by smooth muscle

options.label: C
options.text: It determines the maximum frequency of contractions

options.label: D
options.text: It is absent in the colon

questions.answerText: It determines the maximum frequency of contractions
questions.solutionHtml: n: • BER is generated by Interstitial cells of Cajal • Sets rhythmic depolarization pattern (not actual contraction) • Smooth muscle contracts only when BER reaches threshold

questions.stem: A patient with intracranial hypertension begins vomiting. This likely involves direct stimulation of which center?
questions.solutionHtml: on: • Area postrema is the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ), lacks BBB, sensitive to toxins/pressure • Vagal centers execute the reflex but aren’t the initial trigger

questions.stem: A patient with spinal cord injury above the sacral level cannot voluntarily defecate but has spontaneous bowel movements. Which mechanism remains intact?

options.label: A
options.text: Voluntary relaxation of external anal sphincter

options.label: C
options.text: Local reflex via pelvic splanchnic nerves

questions.answerText: Local reflex via pelvic splanchnic nerves
questions.solutionHtml: n: • The defecation reflex is spinal (S2–S4) mediated, involuntary reflex persists even if higher control is lost.

questions.stem: A patient is treated with both ranitidine (H2 blocker) and vagotomy. Which cell is directly affected by both treatments?
questions.solutionHtml: on: • Parietal cells are stimulated by: o Vagus (via ACh, indirect via GRP → gastrin) o Histamine (H₂ receptor) • Blocking both shuts down acid secretion maximally

questions.stem: In a patient with autoimmune gastritis, which step in vitamin B12 absorption is most likely impaired?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Autoimmune gastritis destroys parietal cells, leading to loss of intrinsic factor → no IF-B12 complex → no absorption in terminal ileum

questions.stem: A patient is found to have iron deficiency anemia post-gastrectomy. Which mechanism best explains this finding?

options.label: A
options.text: Lack of vitamin C reduces Fe³⁺ conversion

options.label: B
options.text: Lack of gastric acid impairs Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ conversion

options.label: C
options.text: Iron transporters are absent in jejunum

options.label: D
options.text: Ferritin binding in colon is impaired

questions.answerText: Lack of gastric acid impairs Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ conversion
questions.solutionHtml: : • Acidic pH helps reduce ferric (Fe³⁺) to ferrous (Fe²⁺) → absorbable form in duodenum • Gastrectomy → hypochlorhydria → ↓ Fe²⁺

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with emphysema has a markedly increased functional residual capacity (FRC). What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: D
options.text: Loss of elastic recoil of alveoli

questions.answerText: Loss of elastic recoil of alveoli
questions.solutionHtml: on: • Emphysema → destruction of alveolar walls → ↓ elastic recoil → lungs “trap” more air → ↑ FRC • A: Resistance affects airflow, not volume • B: Emphysema increases compliance • C: Not characteristic of emphysema

questions.stem: During labored breathing in COPD, which of the following muscles contributes to active inspiration?
questions.solutionHtml: : • Sternocleidomastoid and scalene assist in accessory inspiration • A & B: Expiratory muscles • D: Abdominal muscle → expiration

questions.stem: A patient is mechanically ventilated. His end-tidal CO₂ (ETCO₂) is much lower than arterial CO₂ (PaCO₂). Which condition is most likely?
questions.solutionHtml: on: • Pulmonary embolism → perfusion problem → ↑ physiological dead space • ETCO₂ drops while PaCO₂ stays high → classic PE pattern • B & C: Don’t cause this discrepancy directly • D: Affects oxygen, not CO₂ difference

questions.stem: In restrictive lung disease, lung compliance is decreased. Which pressure-volume change best reflects this?

options.label: A
options.text: Large volume change per small pressure

options.label: B
options.text: Small pressure change per large volume

options.label: C
options.text: Small volume change per large pressure

options.label: D
options.text: Equal volume change for all pressures

questions.answerText: Small volume change per large pressure
questions.solutionHtml: : • Compliance = ΔV / ΔP • ↓ Compliance → need high pressure to cause even small volume change

questions.stem: A neonate with congenital heart disease has normal ventilation but zero oxygenation improvement with 100% O₂. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.solutionHtml: : • In shunt: blood bypasses ventilated alveoli → no oxygenation even with 100% O₂ • A & B: Partial improvement expected • C: High V/Q → dead space

questions.stem: A 50-year-old smoker has an FEV1/FVC ratio of 55%. Which is the most consistent finding?
questions.solutionHtml: : • FEV1/FVC <70% → obstructive pattern • In COPD → air trapping → ↑ RV • C: Seen in restrictive disease • D: Emphysema reduces recoil

questions.stem: A lesion in the pons results in prolonged inspiratory gasps with brief expirations (apneustic breathing). What center is likely damaged?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Pneumotaxic center inhibits the apneustic center • Damage → apneustic breathing pattern • DRG/VRG are medullary (not pons)

questions.stem: Which of the following changes is the most powerful stimulus for ventilation in normal individuals?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Central chemoreceptors respond most to ↑ CO₂ (via pH drop) • PO₂ affects peripheral chemoreceptors, but only when <60 mm Hg

questions.stem: In which scenario is the Hering–Breuer inflation reflex is most significant?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Stretch receptors → inhibit inspiration during overinflation • Protective in deep breaths, not active in quiet breathing

questions.stem: A patient becomes apneic following bilateral carotid body removal. What is the most immediate deficit?

options.label: C
options.text: Loss of response to metabolic alkalosis

questions.solutionHtml: : • Carotid bodies sense hypoxia (↓ PO₂) • Central chemoreceptors detect CO₂/pH, not O₂

questions.stemHtml: The above figure shows three diﬀerent compliance curves (S, T, and U) for isolated lungs subjected to various transpulmonary pressures. Which of the following best describes the relative compliances for the three curves?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) S > T > U

questions.stemHtml: Assuming a respiratory rate of 12 breaths/min, calculate the minute ventilation.

A 67-year-old man has a solid tumor that pushes against an airway, partially obstructing air flow to the distal alveoli. Which point on the line of the O2-CO2 diagram above corresponds to the alveolar gas of these distal alveoli?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A)

questions.stemHtml: Read the image of O2 – Hb Dissociation curve given below. What are the approximate values of Hb saturation (% Hb-O2), PO 2, and O2 content for oxygenated blood leaving the lungs and reduced blood returning to the lungs from the tissues?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C)

questions.stemHtml: Which time points on the below figure (V-Z) are associated with the highest P CO 2 of lung blood and highest PCO 2 of the neurons in the respiratory center?
questions.solutionHtml: n: The basic mechanism of Cheyne-Stokes breathing can be aributed to a buildup of CO2 that stimulates overventilation, followed by a depression of the respiratory center because of a low PCO 2 of the respiratory neurons. It should be clear that the greatest depth of breathing occurs when the neurons of the respiratory center are exposed to the highest levels of CO2 (point W). This increase in breathing causes CO2 to be blown oﬀ, and thus the PCO 2 of the lung blood is at its lowest value at about point Y in the figure. The PCO 2 of the pulmonary blood gradually increases from point Y to point Z, reaching its maximum value at point V. Thus, it is the phase lag between the PCO 2 at the respiratory center and the PCO 2 of the pulmonary blood that leads to this type of breathing. The phase lag often occurs with left heart failure due to enlargement of the left ventricle, which increases the time required for blood to reach the respiratory center. Another cause of Cheyne-Stokes breathing is increased negative feedback gain in the respiratory control areas, which can be caused by head trauma, stroke, and other types of brain damage

questions.stem: A patient is given a drug that preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole of the glomerulus. Which of the following is the most likely immediate effect on GFR?

options.label: A
options.text: Decreased GFR due to reduced renal blood flow

options.label: B
options.text: Increased GFR due to increased glomerular capillary pressure

options.label: C
options.text: Decreased GFR due to mesangial contraction

questions.answerText: Increased GFR due to increased glomerular capillary pressure
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Efferent arteriole constriction → ↑ pressure in glomerular capillaries → ↑ GFR (initially) • A: RBF decreases, but GFR initially increases • C: Mesangial cells not directly involved here • D: There is an effect

questions.stem: A patient is given ACE inhibitors. Which of the following best describes their effect on filtration fraction?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased FF due to increased GFR

options.label: B
options.text: Decreased FF due to decreased efferent arteriole resistance

options.label: C
options.text: No change in FF due to autoregulation

options.label: D
options.text: Increased FF due to decreased renal plasma flow

questions.answerText: Decreased FF due to decreased efferent arteriole resistance
questions.solutionHtml: : • FF = GFR / RPF • ACE inhibitors dilate efferent arterioles → ↓ GFR, minimal change in RPF → ↓ FF

questions.stem: A diabetic patient with blood glucose of 300 mg/dL is noted to have glucosuria. Which of the following best explains the mechanism?

options.label: C
options.text: Exceeding the maximal reabsorptive capacity of glucose transporters

questions.answerText: Exceeding the maximal reabsorptive capacity of glucose transporters
questions.solutionHtml: : • Glucose is reabsorbed by SGLT-2 in PCT • If plasma glucose > transport maximum (Tm) → glucosuria • D: Threshold is normal; it’s just exceeded

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man has a blood glucose level of 180 mg/dL, yet he shows glucose in urine. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Normally, threshold ≈ 180 mg/dL • Glucosuria at threshold suggests early saturation or mutated SGLT proteins (e.g., familial renal glucosuria)

questions.stem: Which segment of the nephron is responsible for actively transporting NaCl into the interstitium and is impermeable to water, contributing to medullary hypertonicity?
questions.solutionHtml: on: • Thick ascending limb (TAL): reabsorbs Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻ → diluting segment • Impermeable to water → generates osmotic gradient for counter-current multiplier

questions.stem: Which nephron segment has urea transporters regulated by ADH to increase urea reabsorption and aid in medullary hypertonicity?
questions.solutionHtml: n: • ADH upregulates UT-A1 and UT-A3 in medullary collecting duct • Promotes urea recycling → ↑ medullary osmolarity → concentrates urine

questions.stem: ABG: pH = 7.30, pCO₂ = 50 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ = 24 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most likely primary disorder?
questions.solutionHtml: : • pCO₂ ↑ (normal = 35–45) • HCO₃⁻ normal = acute • pH ↓ → primary respiratory acidosis

questions.stem: In chronic metabolic acidosis, renal ammoniagenesis increases. What is the primary source of ammonia production in proximal tubules?
questions.solutionHtml: on: • Glutamine metabolism in PCT → NH₃ and α-ketoglutarate • NH₃ buffers H⁺ in lumen → aids acid excretion

questions.stem: A child with hypertension, metabolic alkalosis, and low renin and aldosterone is found to have a gain-of-function mutation in the ENaC channel. What best explains the pathogenesis?

options.label: C
options.text: Increased Na⁺ reabsorption in collecting duct

questions.answerText: Increased Na⁺ reabsorption in collecting duct
questions.solutionHtml: n: • Liddle syndrome: ↑ ENaC activity in collecting duct → Na⁺ reabsorption → ↑ volume, HTN → suppresses RAAS • Also causes K⁺ and H⁺ loss → alkalosis

questions.stem: A child presents with hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and normal blood pressure. Genetic testing shows a mutation in the Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ transporter. Which segment is affected?
questions.solutionHtml: on: • Bartter syndrome = defective NKCC2 in TAL → mimics loop diuretic • Leads to salt wasting, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis without HTN (RAAS activation compensates)

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy receives a subcutaneous insulin injection after a glucose-rich meal. Which of the following best describes the immediate cellular mechanism in skeletal muscle?

options.label: A
options.text: Activation of PKA and cAMP pathway

options.label: B
options.text: Increased GLUT-2 expression on plasma membrane

options.label: C
options.text: Increased GLUT-4 translocation to plasma membrane

questions.answerText: Increased GLUT-4 translocation to plasma membrane
questions.solutionHtml: on: Insulin promotes glucose uptake into skeletal muscle and adipose tissue via translocation of GLUT-4 transporters through tyrosine kinase receptor signaling. • A: cAMP pathway is inhibited by insulin. • B: GLUT-2 is found in liver and pancreatic β-cells, not muscle. • D: Insulin activates, not inhibits, tyrosine kinase.

questions.stem: A patient with primary hyperparathyroidism has elevated serum calcium. Which mechanism best explains the bone resorption seen in this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Direct activation of osteoclasts by PTH

options.label: C
options.text: Indirect activation of osteoclasts via RANKL expression by osteoblasts

options.label: D
options.text: Inhibition of osteoblasts by vitamin D

questions.answerText: Indirect activation of osteoclasts via RANKL expression by osteoblasts
questions.solutionHtml: n: PTH stimulates osteoblasts to express RANKL, which activates osteoclast precursors, leading to bone resorption. • A: PTH does not directly activate osteoclasts. • B: Calcitonin opposes PTH. • D: Vitamin D facilitates mineralization, not inhibition.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman has weight loss, palpitations, and heat intolerance. Her TSH is suppressed, and free T4 is elevated. At the cellular level, thyroid hormones exert their effect by:

options.label: C
options.text: Binding to nuclear receptors and regulating transcription

questions.answerText: Binding to nuclear receptors and regulating transcription
questions.solutionHtml: : Thyroid hormones are lipophilic and bind to nuclear receptors, altering gene expression. • A/B: TSH acts via cAMP, but not T3/T4. • D: Incorrect mechanism.

questions.stem: A man with a pheochromocytoma has episodic hypertension and palpitations. Which of the following best explains his elevated blood pressure?
questions.solutionHtml: on: Pheochromocytomas secrete excessive norepinephrine, which activates α1 receptors causing vasoconstriction and hypertension. • A: β2 causes vasodilation • C: Dopamine acts primarily in kidneys • D: RAS may be secondary but not primary in pheochromocytoma.

questions.stem: In a patient undergoing surgery, cortisol levels rise. What is the primary cardiovascular effect of cortisol during stress?
questions.solutionHtml: n: Cortisol enhances the α1 receptor sensitivity to catecholamines → maintains BP during stress. • A: Aldosterone works independently. • B/D: Opposite of cortisol effects.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with gigantism has elevated IGF-1. The growth-promoting effects of GH are mediated predominantly via:

options.label: D
options.text: GH binding to GPCRs on chondrocytes

questions.solutionHtml: n: GH stimulates liver to produce IGF-1, which promotes bone and tissue growth. • A/D: GH acts indirectly on growth tissues. • C: Not the main mechanism.

questions.stem: A patient with head trauma presents with polyuria and polydipsia. Urine remains dilute even after water deprivation but concentrates after desmopressin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml: : Desmopressin response indicates ADH deficiency, i.e., central DI. • C: Nephrogenic DI would not respond. • A: Presents with water retention. • D: May concentrate partially with water deprivation.

questions.stem: A child with rickets is found to have low serum calcium and phosphate. Which mechanism best describes how vitamin D corrects this?

options.label: A
options.text: Inhibits calcium absorption from the gut

options.label: C
options.text: Stimulates intestinal expression of calcium-binding proteins

questions.answerText: Stimulates intestinal expression of calcium-binding proteins
questions.solutionHtml: : Calcitriol (active Vit D) increases intestinal Ca²⁺ and phosphate absorption via calbindin D expression. • A/B: Opposite of Vit D action • D: Not its function

questions.stem: Which of the following hormones uses the cAMP second messenger system?
questions.solutionHtml: n: ACTH uses Gs protein → cAMP → PKA • A: GH uses JAK-STAT • B: Nuclear receptor • D: Tyrosine kinase

questions.stem: A hormone binds a Gq-coupled receptor, activating phospholipase C. Which of the following second messengers is subsequently increased?
questions.solutionHtml: : Gq → PLC → IP3 & DAG → Ca²⁺ release • A: Gs pathway • C: Used by NO/ANP • D: Not a second messenger

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman with hypothalamic amenorrhea has low levels of GnRH, LH, FSH, and estradiol. Which of the following best explains the absence of ovulation?

options.label: D
options.text: Excessive androgens from the adrenal gland

questions.solutionHtml: : GnRH deficiency → ↓LH → no mid-cycle LH surge → no ovulation.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man has infertility despite normal testosterone levels. Which testicular cell dysfunction most likely explains his low sperm count?
questions.solutionHtml: n: Sertoli cells support spermatogenesis, secrete inhibin B, and maintain the blood-testis barrier.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old phenotypic female has primary amenorrhea. She has sparse axillary hair and a blind-ending vagina. Karyotype is 46,XY. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml: : Complete AIS = 46,XY with nonfunctional androgen receptors → female phenotype, no uterus, undescended testes.

questions.stem: A rise in estrogen during the late follicular phase leads to a surge in which hormone?
questions.solutionHtml: n: High estrogen → positive feedback on anterior pituitary → LH surge → ovulation.

questions.stem: During the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle, progesterone is responsible for which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml: : Progesterone converts proliferative endometrium into secretory type to support implantation.

questions.stem: Which hormone, secreted by syncytiotrophoblasts, maintains corpus luteum function during early pregnancy?
questions.solutionHtml: : hCG mimics LH to maintain corpus luteum and progesterone production until placenta takes over.

questions.stem: Spermatogenesis occurs in the seminiferous tubules and requires optimal temperature and hormonal support. Which hormone provides negative feedback to the anterior pituitary to regulate FSH?
questions.solutionHtml: : Inhibin B is secreted by Sertoli cells and inhibits FSH production.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy has ambiguous genitalia and hypertension. 17-hydroxyprogesterone is elevated. What enzyme deficiency best explains his findings?
questions.solutionHtml: n: 11β-hydroxylase deficiency → ↓cortisol, ↓aldosterone, ↑11-DOC (mineralocorticoid) → HTN and androgen excess.

questions.stem: A postpartum woman is able to breastfeed her infant despite high prolactin levels during pregnancy not inducing lactation. What hormonal change postpartum permits milk secretion?
questions.solutionHtml: : Estrogen and progesterone inhibit milk secretion despite high prolactin. Their fall after delivery → lactation starts.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with hot flashes and irregular periods. Lab shows ↑FSH, ↓estradiol. Which is the physiological basis for the high FSH?

options.label: B
options.text: Decreased negative feedback from estrogen and inhibin

options.label: C
options.text: Elevated LH stimulating the anterior pituitary

questions.answerText: Decreased negative feedback from estrogen and inhibin
questions.solutionHtml: : Ovarian failure → ↓estrogen and ↓inhibin → ↑FSH and LH due to lack of feedback inhibition.
